quote: In der Variationsrechnung könnte man den Grund- prinzip aufstellen: Die Eigenschaft, Minimalfunktion zu sein, hört nicht eher auf, als 2 Lösungen zu- sammenfallen also bis zu einer discriminirenden Stelle.
english: In the calculus of variations one could set up the basic principle: the property of being a minimal function does not cease before 2 solutions coincide, i.e. up to a discriminating point.
topic: Notes on branch points and the variational calculus (minimal functions, Lagrange's equation, constructibility of fields), on characteristics of first-order partial differential equations as lines along which solutions stay unbranched, and a plan to characterise multiple Poincaré limit cycles in order to prove that the number of cycles is finite.

triage.modern_statement: In modern terms, Hilbert is guessing at the Jacobi (conjugate-point) principle of the classical calculus of variations. Take an extremal of a regular one-dimensional variational problem, i.e. a solution of the Euler–Lagrange ('Lagrange's') equation, with its left endpoint fixed. The guess is that it stays a (weak) minimiser as its right endpoint moves forward, and stops being one only at the first conjugate point. That is the first point where the extremal meets the envelope (discriminant locus) of the one-parameter family of neighbouring extremals from the same starting point. There, two infinitely near solutions of the boundary-value problem merge ('2 Lösungen zusammenfallen'). In other words: the strengthened Legendre condition plus having no conjugate point is sufficient for a minimum, and going past a conjugate point destroys the minimum (the necessity of Jacobi's condition). The link to Hilbert's notes on 'constructibility of fields' is that a Weierstrass field of extremals can be built around the arc exactly as long as no conjugate point lies on it.
triage.answered_by: This was already classical when Hilbert wrote it, not something solved later. Jacobi set out the conjugate-point condition in 1837, and Weierstrass gave rigorous necessity and sufficiency proofs in his lectures in the 1870s–80s. The envelope theorem, which explains why the minimum fails beyond the point where the extremal touches the envelope, was proved in general by Darboux and Zermelo (1894) and Kneser (1898). Hilbert's own invariant integral and field construction (1900) became a standard route to the sufficiency half. The note is not one of the 23 problems as such. It falls within the broad programme of Problem 23 (development of the calculus of variations), and its ideas continue in Morse theory (Morse index theorem).

evidence.claim: MathWorld: the envelope theorem links evolutes to individual extremals in the calculus of variations. Darboux and Zermelo proved it in general in 1894, and Kneser in 1898. It concerns one-parameter families of extremals from a fixed point that have an envelope.

Wikipedia (Envelope): in a Riemannian manifold, if a family of geodesics from a point P has an envelope, P has a conjugate point wherever a geodesic of the family meets the envelope. The page says the same holds more generally for families of extremals in the calculus of variations.

Liberzon's lecture notes: conjugate points are defined through intersections of neighbouring extremals (solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equation) via the Jacobi accessory equation. They give a sufficient condition for a weak minimum (no conjugate points). Example: on a sphere, great-circle extremals from a point meet again at the antipode.
Course notes on sufficient conditions: if the Jacobi equation has no points in [a,b] conjugate to a, then (with the Legendre condition) the extremal is a relative minimum.
Wikipedia: Hilbert's 23rd problem is not so much a specific problem as an encouragement to develop the calculus of variations further. Its later development includes work by Marston Morse.

triage.why: The 'basic principle' Hilbert proposes matches the classical Jacobi conjugate-point theory. In that theory an extremal stays minimising up to the first conjugate point, where it touches the envelope (discriminant) of neighbouring extremals and where nearby solutions of the boundary-value problem merge. The conjugate-point condition itself goes back to Jacobi and Weierstrass. The search confirmed the envelope theorem (Darboux/Zermelo 1894, Kneser 1898) and the textbook sufficiency result for Jacobi's condition. I did not retrieve sources for the 1837 and Weierstrass dates; those come from standard history. The question is settled textbook material for classical regular problems, though conjugate points are still studied in generalised settings (singular extremals, optimal control). The note is in German, which made it harder to pin down. Confidence is medium rather than high for two reasons: the note is short and informal, and the exact meaning of 'discriminirende Stelle' (conjugate point versus another kind of branch point) cannot be fully confirmed from the page alone.
